key: Ask whether the cells still stick together. Ductal cells keep E-cadherin, so they fill ducts, necrose, calcify and form masses; lobular cells lose E-cadherin, so they fall apart, rarely calcify and spread in single file.
items: Comedo necrosis in the center of the duct
Cohesive ductal cells pack the duct so tightly that the central cells lose their blood supply and die.
Calcified comedo debris is the mammographic signature of ductal carcinoma in situ.
Cohesive DCIS cells bridge the duct and leave sieve-like holes, a ductal architecture.
Invasive ductal carcinoma provokes a dense fibrous stroma that makes a gritty, spiculated mass.
Paget cells come from an underlying ductal carcinoma that has traveled up the lactiferous ducts.
Invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type makes up about three quarters of cases.
Lobular cells lose the CDH1 product, which is why they no longer hold together.
Dyscohesive lobular cells slip through the stroma one behind another instead of forming glands.
Incidental finding on a biopsy done for another lesion
LCIS rarely calcifies or forms a mass, so it is usually discovered by chance.
Marks raised cancer risk in both breasts
LCIS is a bilateral risk marker rather than a precursor confined to the biopsy site.
Metastases to peritoneum, ovary and meninges
Invasive lobular carcinoma favors unusual sites such as serosal surfaces and the leptomeninges.
Germline CDH1 with diffuse gastric cancer
Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer families also develop lobular breast cancer through the same adhesion defect.
